title: India's $11-Billion Quick Commerce War Just Got Its Two Biggest Combatants. Kirana Stores Should Be Nervous.
excerpt: Flipkart and Amazon are flooding smaller cities with thousands of dark stores, challenging homegrown startups Blinkit and Zepto in a race that is reshaping how 1.4 billion people shop.
body:
Two years ago, if you wanted milk at midnight in Patna, you drove to the corner shop. Today, Flipkart will bring it to your door in twelve minutes — and so will Amazon, Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy. Welcome to the most expensive grocery race in Asia.

Flipkart, the Walmart-owned e-commerce giant, announced this week that its quick-commerce arm, Flipkart Minutes, has crossed 1,000 micro-fulfilment centres across 130 Indian cities. It is targeting 1,500 within months. Amazon, not to be outdone, said it is expanding its ultra-fast delivery service, Amazon Now, to 300 cities — up from just 15 earlier this year. Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, personally toured one of the company's Indian dark stores during a visit to New Delhi that also saw him announce a $48-billion investment commitment in the country.

The numbers tell the story of an industry in overdrive. Blinkit, owned by Zomato's parent Eternal, leads the market with over 2,200 dark stores and 27 million monthly transacting users, commanding roughly 46 per cent of India's quick-commerce market. Swiggy's Instamart follows with more than 1,100 stores across 129 cities. Zepto, the startup that popularised ten-minute delivery, holds about 24 per cent. Together, these three control 95 per cent of an $11-billion sector that barely existed four years ago.

## Beyond the Metros

What makes the latest expansion different is where it is happening. Flipkart Minutes says 70 per cent of its footprint is in smaller towns and cities, not metros. Tier-II and Tier-III markets on its network experienced a staggering 42-fold growth in volume over the past year. "People in smaller cities build a slightly larger basket," Kunal Gupta, the head of Flipkart Minutes, told reporters, noting that the company has expanded aggressively even in Bihar, one of India's poorest states.



> **"Blinkit, owned by Zomato's parent Eternal, leads the market with over 2,200 dark stores and 27 million monthly transacting users, commanding roughly 46 per cent of India's quick-commerce market."**


Amazon is chasing the same logic. Its existing logistics infrastructure — warehouses, delivery fleets, and a Prime subscriber base of roughly 150 million monthly active users — gives it a readymade runway into cities where Blinkit and Zepto are still thin on the ground. Prime members who start using Amazon Now triple their shopping frequency, the company says.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


## The Dark-Store Economy

India now has more than 6,000 dark stores — neighbourhood-level micro-warehouses purpose-built for speed, not foot traffic. These cramped, windowless spaces, typically 2,000 to 4,000 square feet, stock everything from iPhones to onions and can process an order in under two minutes.

But profitability remains the elephant in the dark store. Swiggy's adjusted EBITDA loss in its latest quarter widened to ₹840 crore, driven almost entirely by new store openings. Bernstein analysts have warned that the overlap among players in major cities is reaching saturation, with multiple dark stores sometimes servicing the same neighbourhood. The question is no longer who can open the most stores, but who can operate 2,000 of them profitably.

The sector is projected to triple to $30 billion by FY28, according to a Flipkart-Bain report. Reliance, through JioMart, has also entered the fray with over 600 stores, leveraging its network of 3,000-plus retail outlets.

## What It Means for the Kirana — and the Diaspora

For India's estimated 12 million *kirana* shops — the family-run corner stores that have defined Indian retail for generations — the implications are existential. Quick commerce is no longer a metro convenience; it is becoming a mainstream retail channel in cities where kiranas have long been the only option.

For the diaspora, the stakes are financial. Zomato, Swiggy, and Flipkart are among the most widely held Indian stocks by overseas Indians. The quick-commerce model India is perfecting — ultra-dense delivery networks optimised for chaotic, high-density urban environments — is now being studied and adapted in the Gulf, Southeast Asia, and parts of Latin America. When NRIs visit home, the shift is visceral: the neighbourhood that once had a single grocer now has four apps promising eggs in eight minutes.

India did not invent quick commerce. But it may be the country that proves whether it can work at continental scale — or whether the math of margins, dark stores, and ₹99 deliveries eventually breaks.
